analysis.one_liner: Loosens federal rules for swap trading platforms, cutting capital buffers and oversight requirements.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and a subcommittee, never received a vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Swap execution facilities are trading platforms where banks and funds swap the risks of financial instruments. This bill would reduce the amount of money those platforms must hold to cover a year of operating costs, let them delegate core regulatory functions to outside vendors, narrow how much trading data they must report across facilities, and lighten the duties of their compliance officers [S2] [S3]. It was introduced by two Republicans in October 2019 and sent to the House Agriculture Committee, which oversees commodity derivatives; it never advanced [S1] [S3] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: The swap trading platforms themselves and the large banks and funds that trade on them benefit, because they would hold less capital, face fewer data-reporting obligations, gain flexibility to hand core functions to third-party vendors, and face lighter compliance officer requirements [S2] [S3]. Speculators also benefit from the removal of the requirement that platforms adopt position limits or position accountability [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Swap trading platforms and derivatives traders

how_it_helps.text: The bill cuts the operating capital requirement for swap execution facilities from covering one year of operating costs to covering a 90-day period or demonstrating an orderly wind-down, whichever is greater [S2] [S3].

It lets registered trading platforms delegate core regulatory functions to any third-party service provider, where currently they may only delegate to other registered entities, and it narrows swap data aggregation and reporting requirements across facilities [S2] [S3].

It eliminates the requirement that swap execution facilities adopt position limitations or position accountability for speculators, and lightens the reporting and certification duties of their chief compliance officers [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the cost would fall on market participants and potentially taxpayers: platforms with thinner capital buffers are less able to absorb losses in a crisis, regulators would have a less complete view of large traders' activity across facilities, and relaxed position-limit requirements could allow concentrated speculation to sway prices in commodity and financial markets. Any failure of an undercapitalized platform in this systemically important market would likely be backstopped by the public.

drawbacks.text: Reducing the required financial resource cushion from one year of operating costs to 90 days or an orderly wind-down leaves trading platforms with less capacity to survive sustained losses, the kind of weakness that can spread stress through financial markets [S2] [S3].

Narrowing large-trader reporting to activity occurring on each individual facility and striking the cross-facility data aggregation provision would give the Commodity Futures Trading Commission a less complete picture of a trader's total market exposure [S3].

Allowing platforms to delegate core regulatory functions to unregistered third-party vendors, and letting compliance officers take on other duties for the same facility, could weaken independent oversight of the platforms' own conduct [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are modest compliance savings for a small number of trading platforms and their large institutional users. The costs are harder to see but larger: thinner capital buffers, less complete data for regulators, and softer internal oversight in a derivatives market that played a central role in the 2008 financial crisis and was rewritten afterward for exactly these reasons. On balance, this is a rule-relief bill for industry whose risks are borne broadly.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee in October 2019 and then to a subcommittee a few weeks later, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Crawford introduced the Swap Trading Improvement Act in the House on October 17, 2019, joined by Rep. Austin Scott of Georgia [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture, the committee with jurisdiction over commodity and swap trading [S1] [S5].
On November 8, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit, and no further action was taken [S5].
The bill had one cosponsor and never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the Dodd-Frank-era rules for swap trading platforms remained as they were, keeping the existing capital, data-reporting, and position-limit requirements in place. Nobody gained what the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing swap-market rules stayed in place

for.name: Rep. Rick Crawford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 17, 2019, to loosen swap execution facility requirements.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee on November 8, 2019, and never brought it to a markup or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred; the only members attached to the bill were two Republicans, and no Democrat signed on, but the committee's inaction cannot be attributed to either party on the record.

industries.note: The bill's main provisions all reduce the platform's own obligations: less required operating capital, more delegation to vendors, lighter compliance officer duties, and narrower data reporting [S2] [S3]. The savings accrue to the platforms, while thinner buffers and blunter regulatory data shift risk onto market participants and, in a crisis, the public.

These are the platforms' customers and the source of the trading the rules govern. Removing the requirement that platforms adopt position limits or position accountability for speculators frees large traders from the main tool used to keep concentrated speculation from moving prices [S2].

The bill lets platforms delegate core regulatory functions to any third-party service provider rather than only to other registered entities, opening new business for compliance and technology vendors [S2] [S3]. Delegated responsibility still rests with the platform, so oversight quality depends on vendors the regulator did not register.

industries.industry: Speculators in commodity and financial markets
industries.note: Eliminating the requirement that platforms maintain position limits or position accountability removes a safeguard aimed at preventing concentrated bets from distorting prices in markets that affect energy, agriculture, and borrowing costs [S2].
